newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FUND VIEW - Asia puts fund managers to the test.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - Asia puts fund managers to the test.

text.p: These are testing times for fund managers investing in Asia.
The region's unsettled financial markets are swinging wildly, requiring funds to take positions on some of the world's most illiquid and volatile stock markets.

Regional traders warned on Friday that buying will remain highly selective following one of the most active weeks in recent memory. They expect to see a continued movement of institutional money into Asia, primarily from Europe but also from the United States.

"We've seen savage movement. What's been happening is an asset allocation in favour of Singapore, and some of it's been coming from Thailand and some of it has been coming from Hong Kong," said Richard Nicholas, managing director at Hambro Pacific Fund Management.
The outlook for both Thailand and Hong Kong remains uncertain, although large foreign funds were reported to be buying whenever Hong Kong's Hang Seng index fell below 13,000.
It closed at 13,113.26 on Friday.
"This is a buying opportunity," said Christopher Ryan, managing director at HSBC Asset Management.

Some regional traders denied that funds were reducing heavily overweight positions in Hong Kong, instead blaming technical factors for some of the weakness. "People aren't necessarily selling off Hong Kong, they're just going for more short-term exposure on the futures," one trader said.
Thailand will continue to gain attention after panic selling and virtual sentiment collapse gripped the market last week.
Moody's Investors Service Inc announced it was placing the kingdom's long-term foreign currency debt under review along with ratings for some of the nation's big banks.
The Stock Exchange of Thailand index (SETI) plunged more than 4.5 percent to a low of 664.45 before recovering to close 15.42 points or 2.21 percent higher at 713.48 on Friday.

"We cannot see any catalyst at the moment that will turn the fundamentals around but with all this hedging activity, the market is liable to (experience) a technical bounce, particularly when the market's down 15 percent in two weeks," said Nicholas.

Stephen Leung, chief investment officer for BZW Asia, said the SETI had scooted through all targets and calling the bottom was extremely difficult. "It's an oversold market. The extent of the oversell is not possible to estimate," Leung said.
Analysts warned that Thailand's baht was key to any recovery, and pressure on the currency would mount until the Bank of Thailand raised interest rates still higher.
Elsewhere in the region, fresh record highs on Wall Street failed to provide support and profit-taking hit many markets waiting for 1996 earnings results.
"This indicates that Wall Street is not the only thing that Asia watches anymore," said Ryan at HSBC.
A general re-rating of the Singapore market will continue, and Indonesia is considered a good bet even though some managers are now wary of the market's 11 percent gain since January 1.

A move into second-line Malyasian stocks was also viewed with suspicion. Patrick Wong, investment director at Jardine Fleming Unit Trusts, said the Kuala Lumpur market was rapidly becoming overstretched at 18-times earnings despite its popularity overseas.
Manila would fall prey to more profit-taking, fund managers said, and further weakness was also expected in South Korea.
"We take this liquidity-inspired rally with a pinch of salt," said Nicholas.
